item.title: What to Expect During a Kitchen Cabinet Installation
item.description:
By the Editorial Team | Published: July 2026 | Last Updated: July 2026

The Day the Kitchen Becomes a Kitchen

Cabinet installation is the moment a kitchen renovation stops being demolition and dust and starts looking like a kitchen again. It is also the phase homeowners understand least - they choose the cabinets, then a crew arrives and, some days later, the boxes are on the walls, level and aligned. What happens in between follows a precise, repeatable sequence, and knowing that sequence turns an anxious wait into an informed one. Understanding what to expect - the order of operations, the preparation that must precede it, and the coordination that must follow - is what lets a homeowner recognize good work as it happens and spot problems early. The detailed, step-by-step version of that process is laid out in the kitchen cabinet installation process; this primer maps the whole experience around it.

Before Anything: The Room Must Be Ready

Cabinets cannot go onto a wall that is not prepared, and the readiness work happens before installation day. Old cabinets are removed, walls are repaired and often painted (at least the areas that will be hidden), flooring decisions are settled, and the rough-in for plumbing and electrical is positioned for the new layout. Critically, the installer needs to know where the wall studs are and whether the walls and floor are reasonably flat and square - because cabinets are heavy, must be anchored into framing, and must end up level regardless of how uneven the room is. A room that is not ready turns installation day into a delay.

The Installation Sequence

Professional cabinet installation follows an order dictated by physics and practicality. The high points, roughly in sequence:

Step What happens Why the order
Layout and high point Level lines snapped; floor's high point found Everything references these lines, not the floor
Upper cabinets first Wall cabinets hung to the level line No base cabinets in the way to reach over
Base cabinets Set, leveled with shims, joined together Level bases are the counter's foundation
Fillers and scribing Gaps to walls closed and fitted Walls are never perfectly straight
Doors, drawers, hardware Fronts hung and adjusted; pulls installed Alignment is the visible quality signal
Countertop templating Counters measured against set cabinets Counters can only be templated once bases are final

The two details that most surprise homeowners are that uppers go up before bases, and that the floor is largely ignored in favor of a level line - because a floor is rarely level, and hanging cabinets to it would telegraph every dip. The whole install references gravity, not the floor.

Why Level and Scribe Matter So Much

Two words define quality cabinet installation: level and scribe. Cabinets that are not perfectly level produce doors that swing open or shut on their own, drawers that don't sit flush, and - worst of all - countertops that cannot be installed correctly on top of them. Scribing is the craft of fitting cabinet edges and fillers to walls that are never truly straight, so the finished run looks seamless rather than showing tapering gaps. These are the details that separate a professional installation from an amateur one, and they are invisible when done right and glaring when done wrong.

What Comes After the Boxes Are Up

Installation does not end when the cabinets are anchored. The countertop process begins only after the bases are set and level, because counters are templated to the actual installed cabinets, not the drawings - a fabricator measures the real run, then returns days later to install the finished tops. After counters come the backsplash, the plumbing and appliance hookups, and the final adjustments to doors and drawers. Understanding that the cabinets are one stage in a coordinated finish sequence - not the finish line - is what keeps expectations realistic about when the kitchen is truly done.

Recognizing a Good Installation

A homeowner does not need to be a carpenter to judge the result. The signs of quality are visible: cabinet doors aligned with even gaps (called reveals) around and between them, drawers that open smoothly and sit flush, cabinet runs that are level and plumb, filler pieces fitted tightly to walls with no tapering gaps, and no visible fasteners or damage. The signs of trouble are equally visible: doors out of alignment, gaps to the wall, cabinets that rock or feel loose, and drawers that catch. Knowing what good looks like - and that so much of it depends on the installer's skill and the preparation beforehand - is the homeowner's best protection, and it starts with understanding the full installation process from the ground up.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does kitchen cabinet installation take?

For a typical kitchen, the cabinet installation itself often takes a few days, though it varies with the size and complexity of the layout. That window covers hanging and leveling the boxes and fitting fillers; the countertop, backsplash, and final hookups happen afterward on their own timelines, so the full kitchen finish stretches well beyond install day.

Do upper or base cabinets get installed first?

Uppers first, in professional practice - hanging the wall cabinets before the bases are in place means the installer isn't reaching awkwardly over base cabinets and countertops. It surprises many homeowners, but it is the standard and more precise sequence.

Why don't installers just follow the floor?

Because floors are almost never level, and hanging cabinets to a sloping floor would leave counters out of level and gaps everywhere. Installers snap a level reference line and set everything to that, shimming the bases up from the floor's high point so the finished run is true regardless of the floor.

What is scribing?

Scribing is fitting a cabinet edge or filler strip precisely to a wall that isn't straight, trimming it to follow the wall's contour so the joint looks tight and seamless. Since walls are never perfectly flat, scribing is what makes a professional installation look built-in rather than approximate.

Can countertops be installed the same day as cabinets?

Generally no - countertops are templated (measured) against the actual installed and leveled base cabinets, then fabricated and installed days later. The cabinets must be final before the counter can be measured, which is why the counter is a separate, later step.

How do I know if my cabinets were installed well?

Look at the reveals - the gaps around and between doors should be even; drawers should sit flush and glide smoothly; runs should be level and plumb; fillers should meet walls tightly without tapering gaps; and nothing should rock or feel loose. Even gaps and smooth operation are the clearest signs of quality.

What has to happen before installation day?

The old cabinets removed, walls repaired and readied, flooring decisions settled, and plumbing and electrical roughed in for the new layout, with studs locatable for anchoring. A room that isn't prepared turns installation day into a delay, so the prep work is as important as the install itself.

Framed vs. Frameless Cabinet Construction Explained

item.title: Framed vs. Frameless Cabinet Construction Explained
item.description:
By the Editorial Team | Published: July 2026 | Last Updated: July 2026

Two Ways to Build a Cabinet Box

Every kitchen cabinet is a box, but there are two fundamentally different ways to build that box, and the choice between them shapes how the cabinet looks, how much storage it holds, and how it installs. Framed and frameless construction represent two traditions - one rooted in American cabinetmaking, the other in European design - and although a finished kitchen can look similar either way, the structural difference underneath affects nearly every practical aspect of the cabinet. Anyone selecting or installing cabinets benefits from understanding the distinction, because it quietly determines door style options, interior access, and the way the boxes join together on the wall. Grasping it early prevents surprises when the cabinets arrive and go up.

Framed Construction: The Traditional Box

A framed cabinet has a face frame - a flat frame of solid wood attached to the front of the box, like a picture frame around the opening. The doors and drawers mount to this frame, and the frame gives the box rigidity and a sturdy surface to attach hinges to. This is the traditional American style, and it enables the classic looks many people associate with kitchens, including doors that sit within the frame opening (inset) and the visible frame between doors that gives framed cabinetry its characteristic appearance.

The face frame's strength is also its trade-off: it slightly narrows the opening into the cabinet, because the frame overlaps the edges of the box. This means the drawer boxes and the clear access into the cabinet are a bit smaller than the full width of the box. For most homeowners the difference is minor, and the frame's rigidity and traditional look are worth it - but it is the defining characteristic that separates framed from frameless.

Frameless Construction: The European Box

A frameless cabinet - often called European or full-access - has no face frame. The doors mount directly to the sides of the box, and the entire front of the cabinet is open to the interior. This is the modern, streamlined approach, and it delivers two clear benefits: maximum interior access and storage, since there is no frame narrowing the opening, and a clean, contemporary look with doors that cover the whole box face and sit close together. Frameless construction pairs naturally with the sleek, handleless and slab-door styles common in modern kitchens.

The trade-off is that frameless boxes rely on thicker, sturdier box material for their rigidity, since there is no face frame providing structure, and they demand precise installation - with no frame to absorb small misalignments, frameless cabinets show any unevenness more readily. When installed well, they offer the most usable space and the cleanest lines; when installed carelessly, their tight tolerances are less forgiving.

Factor Framed Frameless
Face frame Yes - solid wood frame on front None - doors mount to box sides
Interior access Slightly narrowed by the frame Full width - maximum storage
Look Traditional; visible frame between doors Modern; doors nearly touch
Door options Inset, partial and full overlay Full overlay only
Installation tolerance Frame forgives small misalignments Less forgiving; precision matters

How the Choice Affects Installation

The framed-versus-frameless decision reaches all the way to install day. Framed cabinets are joined to each other through their face frames, which give a solid, thick surface to clamp and fasten together, and the frame provides a little tolerance to absorb the imperfections of real walls. Frameless cabinets join box-side to box-side and depend on the boxes being set perfectly plumb and aligned, because any deviation shows in the tight gaps between their full-overlay doors. Neither is harder to install in absolute terms, but frameless construction rewards precision more strictly, which is one reason installer skill matters and why the overall installation process deserves attention regardless of box type.

Which Is Right for a Kitchen?

Neither construction is universally better; they serve different priorities. Framed cabinets suit traditional and transitional kitchens, homeowners who want inset doors, and those who value the frame's forgiving sturdiness. Frameless cabinets suit modern kitchens, anyone maximizing storage in a smaller space, and those drawn to clean, contemporary lines. Many kitchens today use frameless for its space and looks; many others choose framed for its traditional character and door flexibility. The right answer follows the kitchen's style and the household's storage priorities - and either way, the quality of the finished kitchen depends as much on how well the boxes are installed as on which type they are.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the main difference between framed and frameless cabinets?

Framed cabinets have a solid-wood face frame on the front that doors mount to; frameless cabinets have no frame, with doors mounting directly to the box sides. That single structural difference drives their look, storage, door options, and installation behavior.

Which offers more storage, framed or frameless?

Frameless - without a face frame narrowing the opening, the full width of the box is accessible, giving slightly more usable space and wider drawers. It's one of the main reasons people choose frameless in smaller kitchens where every inch counts.

Are frameless cabinets better quality?

Not inherently - quality depends on materials and construction, not the style. Frameless boxes use thicker material for rigidity since they lack a frame, while framed boxes gain rigidity from the frame. Both can be excellent or poor; the construction type is a design choice, not a quality ranking.

Can I get inset doors on frameless cabinets?

No - inset doors (which sit within a frame opening) require a face frame, so they are a framed-cabinet feature. Frameless cabinets use full-overlay doors that cover the box face. If inset styling is the goal, framed construction is required.

Does the construction type affect installation?

Yes - framed cabinets join through their sturdy face frames and tolerate small wall imperfections better, while frameless cabinets join box-to-box and demand precise, plumb setting because their tight door gaps reveal any misalignment. Frameless rewards installer precision more strictly.

Which style is more modern?

Frameless reads as the more modern, European look - clean lines, doors that nearly touch, and a seamless face - and pairs naturally with contemporary slab and handleless doors. Framed cabinetry reads more traditional, with its visible frame and inset option.

How do I choose between them?

Follow the kitchen's style and your storage priorities: framed for traditional or transitional looks and inset doors, frameless for modern lines and maximum interior space. Both install well when done by a skilled installer, so the decision is about aesthetics and access rather than one being universally superior.

Stock, Semi-Custom, and Custom Cabinets Explained

item.title: Stock, Semi-Custom, and Custom Cabinets Explained
item.description:
By the Editorial Team | Published: July 2026 | Last Updated: July 2026

Three Tiers, One Kitchen

When people shop for kitchen cabinets, they quickly encounter three words that sort the entire market: stock, semi-custom, and custom. These are not brands or styles but tiers of how the cabinets are made and how much they can be tailored, and the tier a homeowner chooses shapes the price, the wait, the fit, and the range of options more than almost any other decision. A kitchen can look beautiful at any of the three levels, but the amount of money, time, and flexibility involved differs dramatically. Understanding the tiers before shopping prevents both overpaying for customization that isn't needed and straining against limits that a higher tier would have solved.

Stock Cabinets: Ready-Made and Fast

Stock cabinets are pre-manufactured in standard sizes and finishes and kept ready to ship or pick up. They come in fixed width increments - typically jumping in three-inch steps - and a limited menu of door styles and colors. Their virtues are price and speed: because they are mass-produced and inventoried, they are the most affordable option and the fastest to obtain, often available almost immediately. For budget-conscious renovations, rental properties, and kitchens whose layouts fit standard sizes, stock cabinets deliver a complete kitchen at the lowest cost.

The limitation is flexibility. Because they come only in standard sizes, gaps between the cabinets and the walls are closed with filler strips rather than custom-fitted boxes, and the size jumps can waste space in a room whose dimensions fall between increments. The door styles, finishes, and internal options are whatever the manufacturer offers, with no substitutions. For many kitchens this is perfectly adequate; for unusual layouts or specific tastes, it can feel confining.

Semi-Custom Cabinets: The Flexible Middle

Semi-custom cabinets start from standard sizes but allow a meaningful degree of modification - depth changes, some width adjustments, a much wider range of door styles, finishes, and interior storage options, and add-ons that stock cabinets don't offer. They occupy the popular middle ground: more expensive and slower than stock, because they are made to order, but far more affordable and quicker than full custom, while offering enough flexibility to handle most kitchens well.

This tier is where many renovations land, because it balances cost against customization. A homeowner can get the door style they want, in the finish they want, with the drawer and organizer options they want, and modest sizing adjustments to fit the room - without paying for a fully bespoke kitchen. The trade-off is that the flexibility still operates within the manufacturer's catalog of options; it is broad, but it is not unlimited.

Tier Flexibility Cost and wait Best for
Stock Fixed sizes and finishes Lowest, fastest Budget jobs, standard layouts
Semi-custom Modifications within a catalog Moderate Most renovations
Custom Built to any spec Highest, longest Unusual layouts, exact vision

Custom Cabinets: Built to Order

Custom cabinets are built specifically for one kitchen, to any dimension, style, material, and configuration the homeowner and maker devise. There are no standard-size constraints - every cabinet can be sized to the exact millimeter of the space, unusual layouts and odd angles are accommodated, and the door styles, woods, finishes, and internal fittings are essentially unlimited. This is the tier of maximum flexibility and the highest price, with the longest lead time because everything is fabricated from scratch for the project.

Custom cabinetry makes sense for kitchens with unusual shapes or ceiling heights that standard sizes cannot serve gracefully, for homeowners with a specific vision that catalogs cannot match, and for those who want cabinetry fitted so precisely that filler strips and wasted space largely disappear. It is the most expensive route, and for a straightforward kitchen it can be more than is needed - but where the room or the vision demands it, nothing else delivers the same result.

How the Tier Affects Installation

The tier even influences install day. Stock and semi-custom cabinets arrive as standard boxes that the installer fits to the room using filler strips and scribing, closing the inevitable gaps between standard sizes and real walls. Custom cabinets can be built to the room's exact dimensions, reducing fillers and gaps - but they demand equally precise installation to honor that fit. Whatever the tier, the finished result depends on how well the boxes are set, leveled, and fitted, which is why the installation process matters at every price point, not just the premium end.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between stock, semi-custom, and custom cabinets?

Stock cabinets are pre-made in standard sizes and finishes; semi-custom start from standard sizes but allow modifications from a catalog of options; custom are built to any specification for one kitchen. The tiers rise in flexibility, price, and lead time from stock to custom.

Which cabinet tier is most affordable?

Stock, by a clear margin - because the cabinets are mass-produced and inventoried, they cost the least and are available fastest. They suit budget renovations and standard layouts, closing gaps to walls with filler strips rather than custom-fitted boxes.

What does semi-custom actually let me change?

Typically door styles and finishes across a wide range, interior storage and organizer options, some depth and width adjustments, and various add-ons - all within the manufacturer's catalog. It offers most of the flexibility homeowners want without the cost of full custom.

When is custom cabinetry worth it?

When the kitchen has unusual dimensions, angles, or ceiling heights that standard sizes serve poorly, or when a homeowner has a specific vision catalogs can't match. Custom fits the space exactly, minimizing fillers and wasted space, at the highest price and longest wait.

Do stock cabinets look cheap?

Not necessarily - many stock lines look excellent in the right kitchen. Their constraint is fixed sizes and a limited option menu, not poor appearance. Where a layout fits standard sizes and the offered styles suit the taste, stock delivers a handsome kitchen affordably.

Which tier do most renovations use?

Semi-custom is the popular middle ground for many renovations, because it balances cost against flexibility - the desired door style, finish, and storage options with modest sizing adjustments, without paying for a fully bespoke kitchen. Stock and custom serve the budget and premium ends respectively.

Does the tier change how cabinets are installed?

Somewhat - stock and semi-custom boxes are fitted to the room with fillers and scribing to close gaps between standard sizes and real walls, while custom boxes can be built to exact dimensions, reducing fillers but demanding precise installation. Good installation matters at every tier.

Semi-custom cabinets start from standard sizes but allow a meaningful degree of modification - depth changes, some width adjustments, a much wider range of door styles, finishes, and interior storage options, and add-ons that stock cabinets don't offer. They occupy the popular middle ground: more expensive and slower than stock, because they are made to order, but far more affordable and quicker than full custom, while offering enough flexibility to handle most kitchens well.

This tier is where many renovations land, because it balances cost against customization. A homeowner can get the door style they want, in the finish they want, with the drawer and organizer options they want, and modest sizing adjustments to fit the room - without paying for a fully bespoke kitchen. The trade-off is that the flexibility still operates within the manufacturer's catalog of options; it is broad, but it is not unlimited.

Tier Flexibility Cost and wait Best for
Stock Fixed sizes and finishes Lowest, fastest Budget jobs, standard layouts
Semi-custom Modifications within a catalog Moderate Most renovations
Custom Built to any spec Highest, longest Unusual layouts, exact vision

Custom Cabinets: Built to Order

Custom cabinets are built specifically for one kitchen, to any dimension, style, material, and configuration the homeowner and maker devise. There are no standard-size constraints - every cabinet can be sized to the exact millimeter of the space, unusual layouts and odd angles are accommodated, and the door styles, woods, finishes, and internal fittings are essentially unlimited. This is the tier of maximum flexibility and the highest price, with the longest lead time because everything is fabricated from scratch for the project.

Custom cabinetry makes sense for kitchens with unusual shapes or ceiling heights that standard sizes cannot serve gracefully, for homeowners with a specific vision that catalogs cannot match, and for those who want cabinetry fitted so precisely that filler strips and wasted space largely disappear. It is the most expensive route, and for a straightforward kitchen it can be more than is needed - but where the room or the vision demands it, nothing else delivers the same result.

How the Tier Affects Installation

The tier even influences install day. Stock and semi-custom cabinets arrive as standard boxes that the installer fits to the room using filler strips and scribing, closing the inevitable gaps between standard sizes and real walls. Custom cabinets can be built to the room's exact dimensions, reducing fillers and gaps - but they demand equally precise installation to honor that fit. Whatever the tier, the finished result depends on how well the boxes are set, leveled, and fitted, which is why the installation process matters at every price point, not just the premium end.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between stock, semi-custom, and custom cabinets?

Stock cabinets are pre-made in standard sizes and finishes; semi-custom start from standard sizes but allow modifications from a catalog of options; custom are built to any specification for one kitchen. The tiers rise in flexibility, price, and lead time from stock to custom.

Which cabinet tier is most affordable?

Stock, by a clear margin - because the cabinets are mass-produced and inventoried, they cost the least and are available fastest. They suit budget renovations and standard layouts, closing gaps to walls with filler strips rather than custom-fitted boxes.

What does semi-custom actually let me change?

Typically door styles and finishes across a wide range, interior storage and organizer options, some depth and width adjustments, and various add-ons - all within the manufacturer's catalog. It offers most of the flexibility homeowners want without the cost of full custom.

When is custom cabinetry worth it?

When the kitchen has unusual dimensions, angles, or ceiling heights that standard sizes serve poorly, or when a homeowner has a specific vision catalogs can't match. Custom fits the space exactly, minimizing fillers and wasted space, at the highest price and longest wait.

Do stock cabinets look cheap?

Not necessarily - many stock lines look excellent in the right kitchen. Their constraint is fixed sizes and a limited option menu, not poor appearance. Where a layout fits standard sizes and the offered styles suit the taste, stock delivers a handsome kitchen affordably.

Which tier do most renovations use?

Semi-custom is the popular middle ground for many renovations, because it balances cost against flexibility - the desired door style, finish, and storage options with modest sizing adjustments, without paying for a fully bespoke kitchen. Stock and custom serve the budget and premium ends respectively.

Does the tier change how cabinets are installed?

Somewhat - stock and semi-custom boxes are fitted to the room with fillers and scribing to close gaps between standard sizes and real walls, while custom boxes can be built to exact dimensions, reducing fillers but demanding precise installation. Good installation matters at every tier.

item.title: How Cabinets Are Measured and Scribed to a Room
item.description:
By the Editorial Team | Published: July 2026 | Last Updated: July 2026

The Reason Cabinets Look Built-In

Walk into a well-finished kitchen and the cabinets appear to have grown from the walls - no gaps, no tapering slivers of light behind them, every run straight and every joint tight. That seamless look is not luck, and it is not because the walls are perfect. Walls are never perfect: they bow, lean, and meet at corners that are rarely square. The reason quality cabinets look built-in is two crafts performed on install day - accurate measurement and skilled scribing. These are the least visible and most decisive parts of a cabinet installation, and understanding them explains both why professional installs look flawless and why careless ones show every flaw.

Measuring: Where the Whole Job Begins

Before a single cabinet is ordered, the kitchen is measured - and it is measured far more carefully than most people imagine. A proper measure records the length of every wall, the height of the ceiling, and the exact position of every obstacle and connection: windows, doors, outlets, switches, plumbing stub-outs, vents, and the locations of the studs the cabinets will anchor into. Crucially, walls are measured in multiple places, because a wall is rarely the same length at the floor as at the counter height, and corners are checked for square. This measurement is the foundation of the entire order and layout; an error here propagates into every cabinet that follows.

The measurement also reveals the room's imperfections in advance - how far out of square the corners are, how much the walls bow, how far off level the floor runs. Knowing these before installation lets the layout plan for them, deciding where filler strips will absorb irregularity and how the runs will be positioned so the imperfections end up in the least visible places. Good installers measure to discover problems early, when they are cheap to solve on paper, rather than late, when they are expensive to solve on the wall.

The High Point and the Level Line

On installation day, measurement continues with two references that govern everything: the floor's high point and a level line. Because floors slope, the installer finds the highest point of the floor along the cabinet run and starts the base cabinets from there - every other base cabinet is then shimmed up to match, so the whole run ends level despite the floor. A level line is marked on the wall as the reference for the upper cabinets and the tops of the bases. From that moment, the cabinets follow the line and gravity, not the floor and not the wall, which is precisely why they end up straight in a crooked room.

Task What it solves
Measure walls in multiple places Reveals bows and out-of-square corners
Locate studs, outlets, plumbing Anchoring points and cutouts planned
Find the floor's high point Sets where leveling starts
Snap a level line Reference for straight, level runs
Scribe fillers and end panels Closes gaps to crooked walls seamlessly

Scribing: Fitting Straight Cabinets to Crooked Walls

Scribing is the craft that makes the seams disappear. A cabinet edge, an end panel, or a filler strip is set against the wall, and because the wall isn't straight, a gap of varying width appears. The installer marks the wall's contour onto the piece - often by running a compass or scribing tool along the wall - then trims the piece to that exact contour so it nestles tightly against the wall with no gap. The result is a joint that looks perfect even though the wall behind it is anything but. Fillers between cabinets and walls, panels at the end of a run, and cabinets meeting a wall at a corner all get scribed, and the quality of that scribing is one of the clearest marks of a skilled installer.

Why This Invisible Work Is Worth Understanding

Measurement and scribing are invisible when done right - which is exactly why they are undervalued and, in careless installations, skipped or rushed. A homeowner who understands them knows what they are paying a professional installer to do: not merely to hang boxes, but to reconcile factory-straight cabinets with a hand-built, imperfect room so the result looks intentional and seamless. This craft is a core part of the installation process, and appreciating it helps a homeowner recognize quality work, ask the right questions, and understand why skilled installation is worth its cost. The tapering gaps and crooked runs of a poor job are simply measurement and scribing done badly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do installers measure walls in more than one place?

Because walls are rarely the same length top to bottom and corners are rarely square. Measuring in multiple places reveals bows and out-of-square conditions, so the layout can plan for them rather than discovering them mid-install when they are costly to fix.

What is scribing on a cabinet?

Scribing is trimming a cabinet edge, end panel, or filler strip to match the exact contour of an uneven wall, so it fits tightly with no gap. Since walls aren't straight, scribing is what makes the joint between cabinet and wall look seamless.

What is the floor's high point and why does it matter?

It's the highest spot along the cabinet run on a sloping floor. Installers start the base cabinets there and shim every other cabinet up to match, so the whole run finishes level despite the floor's slope. Starting anywhere else would leave the run out of level.

Why don't cabinets just follow the wall and floor?

Because walls bow and floors slope, so following them would produce crooked, out-of-level runs and gaps. Installers reference a level line and the floor's high point instead, setting the cabinets to gravity so they end up straight in an imperfect room.

What are filler strips for?

Filler strips close the gaps between standard-size cabinets and walls or between cabinets and appliances. They are scribed to the wall's contour so the gap disappears, which is how standard cabinets fit neatly into rooms that are never standard dimensions.

How can I tell if scribing was done well?

Look where cabinets meet walls and at the ends of runs: the joints should be tight with no tapering slivers of gap, and fillers should sit flush against the wall. Visible gaps that widen along their length are the sign of scribing skipped or done poorly.

Why is measurement so important to the whole job?

Because it's the foundation everything else rests on - the cabinet order, the layout, the cutouts, and the anchoring all depend on accurate measurements. An error at the measuring stage propagates into every cabinet, which is why careful measurement is where a quality installation truly begins.

Coordinating Cabinets and Countertops in a Kitchen

item.title: Coordinating Cabinets and Countertops in a Kitchen
item.description:
By the Editorial Team | Published: July 2026 | Last Updated: July 2026

The Handoff That Makes or Breaks a Kitchen

Cabinets and countertops are two separate trades, installed at different times by different people, and the handoff between them is one of the most consequential moments in a kitchen renovation. Get the coordination right and the counters land perfectly on level cabinets with clean seams and precise cutouts. Get it wrong and the problems are expensive and visible: counters that rock, gaps at the wall, sink openings in the wrong place, and finger-pointing between the cabinet installer and the countertop fabricator. Understanding how the two trades depend on each other - and the strict order they must follow - is what keeps a kitchen's most expensive surfaces from becoming its biggest headache.

Why Cabinets Must Come First - and Be Perfect

The rule is absolute: cabinets are fully installed and leveled before countertops are measured. This is because a countertop is a rigid, unforgiving surface - a slab of stone or a run of solid material cannot flex to accommodate cabinets that are out of level. If the base cabinets are not dead level and properly aligned, the counter placed on top will rock, show gaps, or sit unevenly, and there is no fixing it short of redoing the cabinets. The cabinets are the foundation; the counter only records how well that foundation was built. This is the single strongest reason cabinet leveling matters so much, and why a good cabinet installation is the precondition for a good countertop.

Templating: Measuring the Real Kitchen

Countertops are not cut from the kitchen drawings - they are templated, meaning the fabricator measures the actual installed cabinets to create a precise pattern for the counter. This happens only after the cabinets are set and level, because the template must reflect reality: the true dimensions of the run, the exact positions of walls that were scribed to, the real corners and angles. The fabricator makes the template (traditionally with thin strips or, increasingly, with digital laser measurement), takes it back to the shop, cuts the counter to match, and returns days later to install it. This templating gap - the days between cabinet completion and counter installation - is a normal, unavoidable part of the sequence that surprises homeowners expecting counters the same day as cabinets.

Step When Why it must be here
Cabinets set and leveled First The counter's rigid surface needs a level base
Templating After cabinets are final Template measures the real installed run
Fabrication Days in the shop Counter cut and finished to the template
Counter installation Return visit Set, seamed, and secured to the cabinets
Sink and plumbing hookup After counter is set Cutouts exist only once the counter is in

The Details That Must Be Decided in Advance

Good coordination means several decisions are settled before templating, not discovered during it. The sink type is the biggest one: an undermount sink (mounted beneath the counter) must be on hand for the fabricator, because the counter's cutout and edge polishing depend on the exact sink, whereas a drop-in sink sits on top and is less demanding. The cooktop, faucet holes, and any other cutouts must be specified so they are fabricated into the counter rather than cut awkwardly later. The overhang, the edge profile, and the seam locations are all decided in advance. When these are settled before the fabricator templates, the counter arrives correct; when they are left vague, the result is rework or compromise.

Why Two Trades Must Work as One

The deepest lesson of cabinet-countertop coordination is that although they are separate trades, they succeed or fail together. The cabinet installer's leveling determines whether the counter sits right; the accuracy of the cabinet run determines whether the template is correct; the decisions made before templating determine whether the counter is fabricated properly. When the cabinet installation is precise and the details are settled in advance, the countertop handoff is smooth and the seams are invisible. When the cabinets are rushed or the decisions are vague, the counter - the most expensive surface in many kitchens - pays the price. This interdependence is why the quality of the cabinet installation reaches beyond the cabinets themselves into every finish that follows.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why must cabinets be installed before countertops?

Because a countertop is a rigid surface that cannot flex to fit uneven cabinets. If the bases aren't level and aligned first, the counter will rock or show gaps with no easy fix. The cabinets are the foundation the counter depends on, so they must be final before the counter is measured.

What is countertop templating?

Templating is measuring the actual installed cabinets to create a precise pattern for the counter, rather than cutting from drawings. The fabricator makes the template after cabinets are set, takes it to the shop, and returns days later with a counter cut to match the real run.

Why can't I get counters the same day as cabinets?

Because counters are templated to the finished cabinets, then fabricated in a shop over several days before installation. This gap between cabinet completion and counter install is a normal, unavoidable part of the sequence - the counter simply can't be measured until the cabinets are done.

Do I need my sink before the countertop is templated?

For an undermount sink, yes - the fabricator needs the exact sink to cut and polish the counter's opening to fit it. A drop-in sink that sits on top is less demanding, but having the sink decided and on hand before templating prevents delays and mistakes either way.

What decisions must be made before templating?

The sink type and model, cooktop and faucet hole locations, edge profile, overhang, and seam placement. Settling these before the fabricator templates ensures the counter is made correctly; leaving them vague leads to rework or compromise on the finished surface.

What happens if the cabinets aren't level?

The countertop placed on top will rock, sit unevenly, or show gaps, and there's no good fix short of redoing the cabinet leveling. This is why careful cabinet leveling is the precondition for a proper counter - the counter records exactly how well the cabinets were installed.

Who is responsible if the counter doesn't fit right?

It depends on the cause - poor cabinet leveling points to the cabinet installer, a bad template or fabrication points to the countertop fabricator. Good coordination between the two trades, with precise cabinets and settled details before templating, is what prevents the finger-pointing entirely.
